titleText.es: Creo que la verdad siempre está a medio camino entre las afirmaciones más extremas.
titleText.en: I believe the truth always lies halfway between the most extreme claims.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish text is the exact title attribute in the Spanish archive; the English text is the exact official xkcd title attribute.

regions.labelEs: SEGÚN MI ANÁLISIS, CREO QUE EL GOBIERNO AMAÑÓ EL CHOQUE DEL AVIÓN Y DEMOLIÓ LA TORRE NORTE DEL WTC CON EXPLOSIVOS.

excludedUnits.rationale: This printed English initialism names the World Trade Center and is not a Spanish lexical word.

regions.labelEs: LA TORRE SUR, EN UN PLAN SIMULTÁNEO PERO SIN RELACIÓN CON EL PRIMERO, FUE DERRIBADA POR VERDADEROS TERRORISTAS.

applications.explanationEn: Simultáneo follows plan in the common neutral order for a descriptive adjective.
Simultáneo uses masculine singular -o to match singular masculine plan.
Sin relación con supplies the reusable expression, and el primero fills its required target slot.
El primero stands on its own for the first previously mentioned plan, leaving that masculine noun unstated.
Fue supplies completed past time, and derribada names what was done while matching the feminine thing affected.
Verdaderos is masculine plural to match the plural group described by terroristas here.

regions.labelEs: LOS DEL MOVIMIENTO POR LA VERDAD DEL 11-S REACCIONARON TIBIAMENTE A MI TEORÍA DE COMPROMISO.

applications.explanationEn: Los stands for an understood plural group of people, and del movimiento identifies which people are meant.

applications.exampleEs: REACCIONARON TIBIAMENTE A MI TEORÍA DE COMPROMISO
applications.explanationEn: Reaccionaron a supplies the reusable pattern, and mi teoría de compromiso fills its required target slot; tibiamente separately describes the manner of the reaction.
Tibiamente is built from the feminine adjective form tibia plus -mente to describe how the reaction occurred.

cards.noteEn: Según introduces the source, standard, or evidence on which a statement is based.

example.en: According to the map, we are close.

cards.noteEn: Análisis has the same written form in the singular and plural; the surrounding article or verb shows the number.

example.en: The analysis was brief.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.noteEn: Amañó is the completed-past form of amañar used with él, ella, or formal usted. It suggests secretly arranging an event or result dishonestly.

example.en: The promoter rigged the result.

cards.answerEn: the joke invents a nonsensical midpoint between incompatible explanations of the two tower collapses
cards.noteEn: The speaker applies the idea that truth must lie halfway between extreme claims: one tower is assigned to a staged demolition and the other to real terrorists. Combining mutually exclusive stories does not create evidence, which is why the proposed “compromise” is absurd.
Spanish writes de followed by the masculine singular word el as the single word del.

example.es: El color del coche es rojo.
example.en: The color of the car is red.

cards.noteEn: Demolió is the completed-past form of demoler used with él, ella, or formal usted.

example.es: La empresa demolió el edificio vacío.
example.en: The company demolished the empty building.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

example.en: I need a new backpack.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something has no connection to something else?
cards.answerEn: Use sin relación con, followed by the other thing.
cards.noteEn: Sin marks the absence of a connection, relación names that connection, and con introduces what it would be connected to. All three words stay unchanged.

example.es: Es un problema sin relación con el clima.
example.en: It is a problem unrelated to the weather.

cards.answerEn: to; required after relación before what is connected
cards.noteEn: In tener relación con or sin relación con, con introduces what something is or is not connected to.

example.es: El cambio no tiene relación con el precio.
example.en: The change is not related to the price.

cards.noteEn: Spanish can leave out a masculine noun that is already understood and keep el before the words that distinguish it. English often supplies “the one.”

example.en: I prefer the blue one.

cards.promptEs: el/la/los/las o un/una + adjetivo sin repetir el sustantivo
cards.questionEn: How do you say “the interesting one” or “a small one” without repeating the noun?
cards.answerEn: Keep the article and adjective, omit the repeated noun, and make both agree with that understood noun.
cards.noteEn: The article is a word such as el, la, un, or una. The adjective still changes to match the omitted noun: una pequeña can mean “a small feminine one,” while uno pequeño can mean “a small masculine one.” Context supplies the missing noun.

example.es: Quiero una taza; dame la pequeña.
example.en: I want a cup; give me the small one.

cards.noteEn: After el, primero can stand on its own and refer back to the first previously mentioned masculine item; the name of that item does not need to be repeated.

example.es: Prefiero el primero de los dos planes.
example.en: I prefer the first of the two plans.

cards.answerEn: was (a completed past instance of ser)

cards.questionEn: How do you say that an action is done to someone or something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of ser, then the verb's completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: Spanish calls that completed-action form a past participle, often ending in -ado or -ido. In this passive pattern it changes to match the person or thing: atrapado for one masculine person, atrapada for one feminine person, and plural forms ending in -ados or -adas.

example.en: The letter was sent yesterday.

cards.noteEn: Derribada comes from derribar, ‘to knock down.’ Its -ada ending is used because the thing described is feminine singular, as in la pared; with fue, it says that the thing was brought down.

example.en: The wall was knocked down yesterday.

cards.noteEn: Before a de phrase, los can stand on its own for an understood masculine or mixed plural group instead of introducing a stated noun.

example.es: Los de la oficina ya llegaron.
example.en: The people from the office have already arrived.

cards.promptEs: el/la/los/las + de + grupo o lugar, sin sustantivo expreso
cards.questionEn: How can el, la, los, or las plus a de phrase identify people or things without repeating their name?
cards.answerEn: Use el, la, los, or las on its own, followed by de and the identifying group, place, or source.
cards.noteEn: Choose el, la, los, or las to match the single item or group understood from context. Its name is left out because the context makes it clear; the following de phrase identifies which one or ones are meant.

example.es: Las de mi clase vienen mañana.
example.en: The women or girls from my class are coming tomorrow.

cards.answerEn: for; in support of a cause
cards.noteEn: After a group, campaign, or movement, por can introduce the cause it supports.

example.es: Participan en una campaña por la igualdad.
example.en: They are taking part in a campaign for equality.

cards.answerEn: about the (de + el, introducing a topic)
cards.noteEn: Del combines de and el. After an expression that introduces a subject of discussion, de can mean “about,” so del introduces a masculine topic.

example.en: We talked about the new project.

cards.answerEn: the Spanish abbreviation for the September 11, 2001 attacks
cards.noteEn: Spanish commonly names major dated events with the day number and the month initial. 11-S corresponds to English 9/11 because Spanish puts the day before the month.
Reaccionaron is the completed-past form of reaccionar used with ellos, ellas, or formal ustedes.

example.en: The neighbors reacted calmly.

cards.questionEn: How do you introduce the thing that someone reacts to?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of reaccionar, then a, then the event, idea, or thing prompting the reaction.
cards.noteEn: Reaccionar changes for the person and time. The preposition a remains unchanged before the target of the reaction, even when English also uses “to.”

example.en: Mario reacted to the question.

cards.noteEn: Tibiamente is formed from tibia plus -mente and describes a response lacking warmth or enthusiasm.

example.en: The audience applauded without enthusiasm.

cards.questionEn: How do you turn many describing words into words such as “quickly,” “clearly,” or “probably”?
cards.answerEn: Use the feminine singular form of the describing word and add -mente. If its masculine and feminine forms are identical, simply add -mente.
cards.noteEn: For an adjective that changes, use its -a form: claro becomes clara and then claramente. For one form shared by both genders, probable becomes probablemente. The new word usually describes how an action happens or how the speaker judges a claim.

example.en: Lucía answers clearly.

cards.answerEn: to; required after reaccionar before what prompts the reaction
cards.noteEn: Spanish uses reaccionar a to introduce the event, idea, or thing that receives a reaction.

example.en: She reacted well to the news.

cards.answerEn: often no separate English word; links a noun to another noun that names its type or use
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses de between two nouns where English uses a noun directly before another noun. For example, una taza de café is ‘a coffee cup,’ and material de oficina is ‘office material.’

example.en: I need a coffee cup.

cards.noteEn: Compromiso can mean a commitment. In a disagreement or negotiation, it can instead mean a middle position accepted between competing proposals.

example.es: Buscamos un compromiso entre las dos propuestas.
example.en: We are looking for a compromise between the two proposals.
